title: Knowing Your School
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart argues that the usual quality assurance mechanisms in schools, such as lesson observations, work scrutinies and data drops, produce unreliable information, and that leaders do better to map what is happening through conversation than to weigh it with numbers. Drawing on Matthew Evans's contrast between weighing and mapping, he works through the questions leaders want answered: how happy and motivated children are, how they behave, what they have learned, how motivated and knowledgeable colleagues are, and what teachers do to help pupils understand and behave. For each he explains why the common proxies mislead, for instance that falling suspensions may only mean poor behaviour is tolerated, and lists what leaders might do instead. He uses Dan Pink's drivers and Peps McCrea's motivation framework to give leaders specific things to find out about staff and pupils. He concludes that information must be accurate and acted upon, but that in a calm and purposeful school, investing time in meaningful conversations is a better bet than the cargo cult of usual monitoring.
points: Aggregated happiness or motivation percentages are not actionable; leaders learn more by knowing which individual children are struggling and then exploring why through conversation.
Behaviour data such as exclusions can mislead, because fewer suspensions may signal that poor behaviour is now more tolerated rather than that it has improved.
Work in books and test scores are poor evidence of what children have learned, so the most useful check is what teachers do when children turn out not to understand.
Dan Pink's purpose, autonomy, mastery and belonging give leaders concrete questions to ask colleagues, but surveys will not answer them and conversations only work with underlying trust.
Leaders should visit lessons to build shared understanding rather than to judge, since the quality of teaching cannot be judged reliably.
quotes: When we map territory we are interested in gaining a true and accurate picture. We set out with a range of tools, each designed to chart what we observe in particular ways.

Happiness and motivation cannot be whittled down to a number. Leaders could survey children to see how happy and motivated they are then aggregate this information and assign a percentage to it. But this aggregation wouldn’t be useful.
Fewer exclusions or suspensions over time is not necessarily symptomatic of improving behaviour. It could equally be that poor behaviour is now more tolerated.
Well, yes, but work in a book does not mean that the child still understands days, weeks or months down the line.

Standardised tests rarely measure what has actually been taught and although assigning a number like a standardised score might make it possible to compare performance to other children, it doesn’t tell us anything about whatchildren have or haven’t learned.
Again, the important bit is to get to the bottom of why colleagues feel as they do. Surveys won’t do that. Conversations will, but only if there is underlying trust.
Judgements are unreliable and unhelpful so visiting lessons in this way is simply to build shared understanding and look for ways to help childrento better understand.

Faced with such complexity and uncertainty, pragmatism is the order of the day. Leaders need to act quickly if it appears that children are unsafe or unhappy, but if school is calm and purposeful, we need not fall victim to the cargo cult fallacy of the usual monitoring activities.
